title: Cashing out a winning underdog
question: When a long-shot underdog bet is going well, does cashing it out at the in-play price beat holding it to the end?
rule: $1 on an underdog at 4.0 or longer at its pre-match close. Cash out at half-time, or else at the 70th minute, once DraftKings' in-play chance for it reaches 50%, paying a 5% cash-out fee. Judged on long-run growth at 2% stakes against holding, on at least 300 cash-outs.
verdict_text: No. First, why holding looks so bad: holding these bets lost 25.3% of every dollar, but the sample left out the matches earlier tests had already bought, and those were mostly underdogs leading at half-time. Put them back and holding loses 15.2%; in 2025/26, where no B or C match was left out, 18.6%. Now the test: cashing out once the underdog's in-play chance reached 50%, paying a 5% fee, beat holding by +0.020% bankroll growth a bet at 2% stakes (range −0.022% to +0.062%) on 570 cash-outs: not distinguishable from zero. With the left-out matches back (half-time only, already read, not judged) it was +0.025% on 386 cash-outs. A free cash-out helps a little, because the in-play price slightly overrates a leading underdog; a realistic fee eats that.
sample_note: To avoid buying any match twice, the sample left out the matches earlier tests had already bought (279 at 4.0+, plus a few of design H's). Those were favourites losing at half-time, so the underdogs we left out were mostly ones leading at half-time, and about half of them went on to win. That makes holding look worse here (−25.3% per $1) than backing long shots really is: with them put back, holding returns −15.2%, and in 2025/26, where none of B or C's matches were left out, −18.6%. The comparison between cashing out and holding is still fair, because what was left out depends only on the pre-match price and the half-time score, both known when the rule decides.

why.title: Why holding lost so much
why.text: The sample left out every match designs B, C and H had bought, as pre-registered, so no match was bought twice. B and C's matches were favourites trailing at half-time: underdogs leading at half-time. In 2024/25's eight main leagues that took out most of them, and they won about half the time, so the hold line here is lower than backing every long shot would be. Because the left-out set depends only on the pre-match price and the half-time score, the cash-out against hold comparison is still fair for the matches kept. The rows compare how often the underdog won with the pre-match price's chance (with its margin).

why.title: Is the in-play price right?
why.text: Grouped by DraftKings' in-play chance at the moment the rule looked. Where the underdog was well placed (55% or more at half-time) it won less often than the price said (64.6% vs 72.0%), so selling the bet at that price was a small gain before any fee.

why.title: What the fee does
why.text: A cash-out at a fair price leaves the average return where it was and only cuts the swings. The gain here came from the price overrating the leading underdog by a few points; a 5% fee costs about as much, and at 10% cashing out loses. Nothing changes live.

notes: Entry: $1 on the underdog at its quoted pre-match close (Pinnacle's, else the market average's). The in-play price is DraftKings' moneyline, margin removed, from the odds archive's snapshots at kickoff + 55 min (half-time) and + 85 min (about the 70th minute). Only quotes updated after kickoff and at most 5 minutes old count.
A cash-out pays entry odds x the in-play chance x (1 - fee). The fee stands in for the margin a book takes on a cash-out offer; 5% is the realistic case.

Growth is the long-run rate a bankroll grows at when every bet risks the same share of it (2% here). It is the fair way to compare holding with cashing out, because cashing out mainly cuts the swings rather than the average.

The sample left out every match designs B, C and H had bought, as pre-registered. Those were favourites trailing at half-time, so in 2024/25's main leagues most underdogs leading at half-time are missing. The left-out set depends only on the pre-match price and the half-time score, both known when the rule decides, so the cash-out against hold comparison stays fair for the matches kept; the hold level does not describe 'backing 4.0+ underdogs' in general.

A first run (40706645115) joined a pair that meets twice at the same ground in a season (Scotland, and the Belgian and Greek play-offs) to its first meeting's result: 90 positions. The join now matches the kickoff too, and this file is the rerun with that fix.
